# Jubilees Chapter 43 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Ge'ez MS; cf. 4QJub (Hebrew fragments) | **Section:** Jacob learns Joseph is alive; the family reunited in Egypt

---

**43:1** The news reached Jacob: Joseph was alive — and he was running Egypt. Jacob's heart nearly stopped. Then he came alive: "That's all I needed to hear. My Joseph is alive. I have to see him before I die."

**43:2** Jacob and all his sons packed up and headed for Egypt. They came to Goshen. Joseph came out to meet his father.

**43:3** Joseph threw himself on his father's neck and cried. Jacob held him and said: "I can die now. I've seen your face. You're alive."

**43:4** Joseph brought his father and brothers before Pharaoh. They all bowed.

**43:5** Pharaoh looked at Jacob and asked, "How old are you?" Jacob answered: "One hundred and thirty years of wandering. Not many years, and they've been hard ones — fewer and harder than my fathers had."

**43:6** Pharaoh blessed Jacob and his sons. Then Jacob and his sons sat and ate before Pharaoh.

**43:7** Joseph set his father and brothers up in Goshen — the prime land of Egypt. He kept them fed. The whole family settled there.

**43:8** The famine ground on — Egypt and Canaan both. Joseph kept collecting silver in exchange for grain: Egyptian silver, Canaanite silver, all of it flowing to Pharaoh's treasury.

**43:9** When the silver ran out, the Egyptians came back: "We're dying. We have no more money. Feed us." Joseph said: "Then bring your livestock."

**43:10** They brought horses, donkeys, oxen, sheep, goats — everything they had. Joseph traded food for livestock. By year's end, all their animals belonged to Pharaoh.

**43:11** The next year they came back again: "Nothing left. Just our bodies and our land. Take it — take us. We'll be Pharaoh's slaves as long as we eat."

**43:12** Joseph bought it all — every piece of land in Egypt except the priestly estates, which were already Pharaoh's grant. That arrangement has been Egyptian law ever since.

---

*PNEUMA notes: The reunion between Jacob and Joseph (vv.1-3) is handled with great economy and emotional power. Jacob's "I can die now" echoes Simeon's Nunc Dimittis-like sentiment. His speech to Pharaoh (v.5) — "few and hard" — is one of the most melancholy self-summaries in all of ancient literature.*
